utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were no preliminaries. The Chamber has received a -- a confidential memo, a proofing note for the next witness, who is not seeking protective measures. Then we will wait for Mr. Milovanovic to be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting, just so that the record is complete from yesterday, General Milovanovic informed me yesterday evening that he has received members of the Perisic Defence team and the Karadzic Defence team pursuant to their request and has answered their questions. And the other point I wanted to raise with the Chamber is that General Milovanovic was unable to get through all of the binders. He is prepared to do that over the weekend, and I was going to propose that he be provided that, but perhaps maybe sometime before the end of the day, I could address the Chamber with the remainder of my proposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text will now be handed down to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic. Please be seated. Mr. Milovanovic, if I address you as "Mr. Milovanovic," rather than as "General Milovanovic," this is not in any way expressing disrespect for your rank. I'm used to address witnesses always by "Mr.," unless they appear as expert witnesses, where the title is of direct relevance for the testimony. You're here as a witness of fact, and that's the reason why I address you, as I address all other witnesses, as Mr. Milovanovic. Mr. Groome or Mr. Weber, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you'll now first be examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution. He is at your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you are appearing here today pursuant to a subpoena issued by this Chamber on the 4th of February, 2010; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, you have had a lengthy professional military career. It is important that the Chamber is aware of it, but not necessary that we discuss it in any great detail here. After you arrived in The Hague, were you asked to review a summary of your professional assignments compiled from your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to make corrections to it and then presented with a summary that you considered accurate?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that document number 5286 be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, when it appears on the screen, I'd ask you to review it and tell us is this the document that summarises your professional qualifications. It's a two-page document, General. I will show you the second page in a moment. There's a signature at the top of that page. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders this summary of General Milovanovic's professional assignments into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to add, something that I have forgotten yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P375, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. If you already assign a number and then we'll hear Mr. Milovanovic's observations. The number would be, Madam Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P375, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, if you would like to add anything, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I forgot that in the meantime, in 1971, I completed as a part-time student the JNA school of politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that is now on the record that you'd like to add this to what is in this document. P375 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, are you willing to answer any additional questions regarding your professional career that the Chamber or the Defence may put to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you several video-clips from a documentary directed by Filip Svarm and shown widely on television in Serbia. The name of the documentary is "The Unit." The documentary had three parts. I will structure my questions to you here today around your interview which is contained in the first and second parts of the documentary. I would like to begin by asking you a few questions generally about this interview that you gave for the documentary. First, can you tell us approximately when it was you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure of exact time, but I think it was sometime in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in preparation for this interview, did you review any materials?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that clip, that film.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm asking you now is before you gave the interview that has been video-recorded, did you review any materials to prepare for the questions you were asked on the video?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I did. First of all, the film that I saw yesterday was -- is a compilation of several statements of mine, and then that was turned into a documentary. Now, as for my preparation, nothing special really. There is no archives of the Main Staff of the army, so it's really just recollections. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, one of the first topics you discuss in the documentary is Arkan. I would like to show you a clip from part 1 of the documentary, and I will ask you to comment on certain aspects of it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Laugel to please play clip 65 ter 2608.1 -- I'm sorry, clip 1 of 65 ter number 2608.1. It is a clip that appears in the original documentary at 58 minutes, 15 seconds to 58 minutes, 52 seconds. And for the benefit of the booth, it is marked as clip 1 on the handout given earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Manojlo Milovanovic: By the time I had arrived at the front line on the 11th of May, Arkan had already finished the job in Bijeljina and Zvornik. "Zuti: There were always problems between us and the Republika Srpska army. "Manojlo Milovanovic: Each time the Serbian Volunteers' Guard returned from Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, apart from transporters and tanks, there was always a large number of container lorries in the column and that was their characteristic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, it seems that the first part of your comment was missed by the interpretation. Perhaps it was the less-than-perfect quality of the audio. Do you recall referring to Arkan as being a separate problem at the beginning of that clip? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my first question to you is whether your comments that we've just listened to are accurate and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you say in the clip that "Arkan is a separate problem," can you describe to the Chamber what it is you meant by this. Describe the problem that you believed Arkan represented.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just Arkan, but all paramilitaries that we found in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of them represented a problem. First of all, because they entered the war without authorisation. Second, because the goal of their participation in the war was not some sort of a freedom of Serbian nation or struggle for Serbian nation. The purpose of their participation in the war was to find an occupation and to pump as much wealth out of it as possible. Sometime in 1991 and 1992 paramilitaries were typical for the former SFRY. There were no authorities in -- proper authorities in power in the SFRY at the time. There were many political parties established and all of them were fighting for power, political power. And the quickest and surest way to come to power was to awaken some new patriotism, as a result of which illegal armed groups were established. And they acted against other ethnic group, regardless of which ethnic group that was and whether that ethnic group armed the Serbs in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can I ask you to be precise in who were -- was the victim or victims of the problem that Arkan created, both in terms of ethnicity and both in terms of -- also in terms of geographical location.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the victims were first of all Muslims and then Croats in addition to them. In the territory of the former Serbian Krajina, the victims were Croats. However, when the wealth of Muslims and Croats in certain area disappeared, then it was the Serbs who became victims. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and once that army entered an area --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before -- could I just ask you a few more questions about the nature of the problem and then I'm going to ask you about the response of the Army of Republika Srpska. You refer to the victims or have identified them as Muslims in Bosnia. Can you be a bit more precise in terms of municipalities within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the point in time that I'd ask you to focus on is at the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the conflict officially broke out, that is to say, before the 6th of April in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Arkan personally together with his group of Tigers, that's what his soldiers were known as, he started cleansing Bijeljina. We saw in the first clip that there was persecution of Muslims. We saw that there was a dead man in Bijeljina. And people saw that clip many times. In addition to looting, they also started killing. So I hope I answered your question. You asked for specific examples. Initially --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- Arkan was active only in Bijeljina and nowhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear a public statement made by Arkan speaking about the JNA's garrison commander Colonel Masala with respect to events in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear that public statement of his in 1996, when he declared that Colonel Masala was a traitor of the Serbian people because he prevented him from doing what he wanted to Bijeljina. And Masala was the commander of the JNA garrison there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Arkan go on to say what it was he wanted to do in Bijeljina that Colonel Masala prevented him from doing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say what he was going to do. He simply said -- or rather, I need to describe the context and we may be wasting time. In 1996 there were elections taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. A woman who represented his party, the Party of Serbian Unity, was a candidate among others for the president of Republika Srpska. And in her pre-election speech when she addressed the nation, she glorified Arkan's accomplishments from the struggle of Serbian people in Semberija, Western Bosnia, and so on. I made a call to that TV broadcast and denied any military achievements of Arkan, especially not in Majevica. Then Arkan's reaction followed. He didn't attack me, rather he defended himself. He said that he had not completed his job in Bijeljina only because he had been prevented by a Serbian traitor, Colonel Masala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you go on in the clip to describe how each time the Serbian Volunteers' Guard returned from the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina they had shipping containers as part of their convoy and this was related to looting activity. Have I understood the import of your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the trucks, I personally discovered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was simply -- that was going to be my next question. Is this something that you personally observed? Can you please describe when, where, and what it was that you observed.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of July, 1995, I was in Han Pijesak to see off General Zivanovic, and I was on my way back to Drvar where my command post was. In Obudovac I came across three BOVs, armoured personnel carriers. It was evening and they had rotation lights on. However, between them there were a couple of trucks, say there would be personnel carrier and then a truck or two trucks and then a personnel carrier and so on. So a couple of trucks. And there was a mixed check-point of the army and the police of the Army of Republika Srpska. I stopped at the check-point and I asked the policeman whose personnel carriers those were. And the young man there said, "Arkan's." And I said, "What about the trucks?" And he said, "Also his." I asked him what were they transporting in the trucks. And he said, "I didn't check all of the trucks, just the last one, and there were a lot of appliances there." I realised that this was a case of looting because Arkan had without any invitation previously come to Kljuc and he joined in the combat of the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska in the Storm operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Banja Luka, I asked to meet --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- could I ask you, did you learn where these convoys were going, what was their destination?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were on their way to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this period that you were aware Arkan was transporting looted goods from the conflict area, were there operational border checks at the border between Bosnia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were border crossings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my intention to work with each of the two clips from the first part of this documentary and then tender them as a single exhibit unless the Chamber prefers that I do otherwise. For the sake of a clear record, I refer to the clip I've just used as 65 ter clip 2608.1, clip 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the documentary you say that: "Arkan had already finished the john in Bijeljina and Zvornik." My first question on this basis is -- I'm sorry, on what basis did -- I'm sorry, I think we've covered those next two questions. What I'd now ask you: What was the response of the VRS to the problem of paramilitaries as you have described?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff, or rather, the 12 officers who were to become members of the future Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska gathered in Han Pijesak on the 11th of May, 1992, in the afternoon hours. There were four generals and eight colonels and lieutenant-colonels. All of them were people who by way of various orders and presidential decrees of the JNA were transferred to the military district in Sarajevo. However, by the time when we arrived there on the 11th of May, there had already been issued an order of the Rump Presidency of the former SFRY that the JNA was to withdraw from some areas, but to remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina until 1997 to protect equally interests of all three nations. However, by the time we arrived there it had already fallen apart, that plan. And when we met there, we spent the whole night discussing what to do. It was still not known who was to be the commander, but there was some hints. Since we didn't have any goals for the war and we knew that we were on the brink of the war, we formulated 21 tasks or principles as to what the future army was supposed to do. I would like to reiterate that the Army of Republika Srpska was the seventh and the last armed force that was established in the territory of the former SFRY. It was the last one because before that we had been expecting that the JNA would protect the Serbian nation. However, in 1993 the eighth armed force was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I apologise for interrupting you and I will allow you to make more comments on some of this general background later on, but just in the interests of time was there a -- was one of the tasks that members of the Main Staff or these senior officers that you've spoken about, was one of those tasks to attempt to either subordinate these paramilitaries into regular troops or to expel them from the territory under the authority of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: One of those 21 tasks was to gather, or rather, to call all the commanders of these paramilitary formations and they were at the level of a group and even at the level of a brigade, and to ask them to join the regular Army of Republika Srpska or to place themselves under the command of the Main Staff. Those who refused to do that were to be expelled, and if they were to put up armed resistance, they were to be defeated. Based on that decision, General Mladic, on the 28th of July, issued an order concerning this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you back to one of your previous questions. You asked, in relation to the looted goods, whether there were operational border checks at the border between Bosnia and Serbia. And then the answer was: "Yes, there were border crossings." Now, that seems not to be unambiguous. Therefore, crossing a border could be a place where people are crossing and where there are checks, although that's not what the answer says. So I'm not certain that the answer is an answer to your question. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, you've heard Judge Orie's request for a clarification. Can you describe what was -- what precisely was at the border between Bosnia and Serbia? What would -- and who staffed that border crossing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Border crossings were organised in a typical manner. There were police there present to check persons and there were also customs officer to check what was the goods that were transported. Normally, first the police would check your personal documents and then customs people would check the goods. As for the Republika Srpska, we had joint police, civilian and military police there. The military police was there because there was an order of the army commander, General Mladic, that all men fit for military service had to remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were not allowed to leave the territory, because they could be mobilised. This is why military policemen were present at all border crossings who turned back --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're asking -- the interpreters are asking if you could speak more closely to the microphone. Now, General, on the -- were the police that were at the border, were there Serb police? In other words, were there members of the Ministry of Interior police of Serbia on the Serb side of that border?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I crossed, I saw people in blue uniforms, which means that they were police members, members of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, returning to dealing with paramilitaries, are you familiar with a person by the name of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have a personal encounter with him with respect to this effort to deal with the problem of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had contacts with Captain Dragan by way of means of communication and also by correspondence. When we decided to expel him as well, I was tasked with doing that and I did it in a military way. I issued -- I gave him an assignment and I told him if he were to complete it, then he could remain in the Army of Republika Srpska, and if he were not to complete it, he had to leave. He didn't complete his assignment and he had to get his things and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, can we just get some basic information about this. Can we get an approximate date, your best recollection of the date, and the precise location of where this interaction between you and Captain Dragan took place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Captain Dragan only once in my life, and that was at a -- at the parade of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 28th of June. It wasn't really a personal contact. He just was part of that parade that passed by the Main Staff of VRS, and then later on, when ARSK was established, the Army of Krajina, I gave him an assignment to track down and to destroy, to eliminate, one of the paramilitary leaders who was active in the villages in that area. If necessary, I can give you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness also tell us the year. I'm sorry to interrupt. You talked about the 28th of June, of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28th of June, 1995. As for my contact by correspondence and by radio with Captain Dragan, that was in June of 1992, at the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you finish your answer to -- in respect of the name you said you could give to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave him an assignment to eliminate Naser Oric, the commander of Muslim forces who were active in the central Drina Valley area. From March of 1992 -- rather, from February of 1992 to March of 1993, he destroyed about 156 Serbian villages and killed about 3.200 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you were -- refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I check, 28th of June, and then the contact by correspondence and radio, that was at the end of -- I thought I heard something different but if it's correct then I -- was it the end of June or was another year mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps I could clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Milovanovic, I asked you about the 28th of what year, and then you said 1995. Then you said, "As for my contact by correspondence and radio," you said, "that was at the end of" -- could you please repeat what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My contact by radio and by correspondence or by dispatches with Captain Dragan took place in the second half of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I heard the 1992. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to just focus precisely on this period of time in June of 1992 for the moment. Do you know where Captain Dragan was active at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until then Captain Dragan was active in the area of the Knin Krajina. Once the Vance-Owen Plan was implemented and UNPA zones were created in Croatia, they were to be some sort of safe havens provided by the UN to the Serbian people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But at the end of June, where was -- where was Captain Dragan, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Captain Dragan moved on to the Zvornik area, to a place called Divic. That's some 8 to 10 kilometres to the south of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when he was in Zvornik, is this also in the end of June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the location which the decision was taken that he must be expelled from?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The decision was made at the Main Staff. He headquartered himself in Divic and established a training camp for members of a sabotage unit or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate size of Captain Dragan's unit when it was in Divic in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already told you that I gave him an assignment. The assignment was given to him by way of a dispatch. He told me that he would carry out an assignment, but he asked for some resources which I couldn't provide, not even an American army had that kind of equipment, special radios, special explosives, special rifles that I had heard of for the first time at that time. We scheduled a meeting in Milici, he and I. I came to Milici and he wasn't there. The people who were there told me that he had to travel to Zvornik and that he would be waiting for me there. I went to Zvornik, he wasn't there either. I realised that the man was making a fool out of me. In Zvornik I was told that he had gone to Divic. I went to Divic, he wasn't there either. In Divic I found 20-odd people with red berets. Their uniforms resembled the ones that he had in Knin. So I said to these guys -- I asked them where they were from. Most of them were from Serbia. Some were from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And there were even our people from Republika Srpska. I told them, "You go back to your units or to your homes and tell Captain Dragan that he needs to disappear from here as well." I went back to the Main Staff on the same day, and on television I saw that Captain Dragan was to have a programme where he talked about a fund that was to take care of the wounded people in that area. That's all I knew about Captain Dragan --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and the one time that I saw him was in that parade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you form an opinion with respect to the professionalism of the 20 men with red berets that you found in Divic? Were they, in your view, professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not professional soldiers. Later on, the people who observed this training of his told me that, for example, he trained those people to jump out of cars in high chase and to do some activities that were anything but training them to use a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the second area you discuss in the documentary is your first meeting with the accused in this case, Jovica Stanisic. I'm going to ask you to look at the monitor in front of you as this is played.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Laugel to now play 65 ter 2608.1, clip number 2. This second clip is 45 seconds long and it commences, on the original tape, 1 hour, 4 minutes in the completed version of the documentary. It is also clip 2 in the handout to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Manojlo Milovanovic: Badza was in uniform and Stanisic in plain clothes. I asked General Panic who these people were. He told me that it was Stanisic - he only said that he was from the State Security Service, he did not say that he was the chief of anything else. I was astounded by Stanisic's knowledge about our situation Podrinje. Some things he even knew better than I did. He knew who was fighting in which village, who was in command, who ... I really was a bit amazed."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that we have viewed 65 ter 2608.1, clip number 2, could you please tell us to the best of your recollection when this meeting occurred.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the meeting occurred at -- on the 23rd of January, 1993, at the river Tara --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: At Mount Tara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us the precise name of where the -- or the location where the meeting was held. Was it held in a particular building?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Hotel Omorika, Mount Tara, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now, General, are your comments as recorded in this clip accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the person that you describe as Badza, do we see him at all in this documentary or in that last clip?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to tell you that on the screen I wasn't able to see when the translation of the spoken parts ends. In any case, one can see Badza at the very beginning of the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the first person that is visible is Badza, the person you refer to as Badza?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us how was he dressed during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The same way we could see him on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have -- did you ever say anything to him or did he ever say anything to you over the course of this meeting or in the time before or after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We greeted each other at the meeting. We listened to Jovica, and General Panic, Badza, he, and I discussed matters whilst the other generals and colonels worked on other issues in different rooms. As you could see on the footage, I was quite amazed with the extent of Stanisic's knowledge and information about particular areas in Bosnia. I wasn't very familiar with Eastern Bosnian. I was quite amazed to hear him speak about the the village of Klotijevac, which is close to Skelani. Following that, I asked General Panic who this person was. He told me that he was from the police, although he did not specify what his name was. I asked Badza who he was. He said, "I arrived here with the boss." Later on in the evening, when I returned to the Main Staff, I told everyone what I could see at Mount Tara. Describing Jovica, they told me, "Well, that was Jovica Stanisic, the head of the state security sector in Serbia." Badza did not tell me that. It was the people at the Main Staff who shared that information with me. That was my first encounter with Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at the meeting in the Main Staff afterward, was there any discussion about who Badza was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when Badza made the statement about "here with the boss," did he make any gesture indicating who he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He did not, otherwise I would have concluded there and then that Jovica was his boss. He merely said, "I'm here with the boss."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And from what you could see, was there anyone else with Badza that appeared to come or leave with Badza or associate with him over the course of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, again I have a problem with the monitor. I can't see -- I can't follow the transcript, hence I can't see when interpretation is finished and when I can start answering. As I said, save for Badza and Jovica, there was no one else with them. Thank you. It was Panic, Jovica, Badza, and I sitting around the table, the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, after this meeting, did you yourself, based on your own observations, form an opinion with respect to the relationship between Badza and Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I never thought about those people again until I met Jovica later on at a number of other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Badza ever tell you what his responsibilities were or what his job was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We never discussed his or my job. I knew that Badza, at the time, commanded some special units or that he was responsible for the special units of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the MUP of Serbia has two divisions, the public security sector and the state security sector. Do you know whether the public security sector has special units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't familiar with the structure of the Serbian MUP. I was familiar with the structure of the RS MUP, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the RS MUP public security sector have special units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It had two special police brigades which were mostly used in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders these two clips from 65 ter 2608.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Two clips of 65 ter 2608.1 become Exhibit P376, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P376 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I would now like to play you a longer clip in which you talk about an operation known as Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that Mr. Laugel now play 65 ter 2609.2, clip 1. It is from the second part of the documentary "The Unit." It is a clip that commences at 23 minutes, 5 seconds, of the original documentary and ends at 25 minutes, 33 seconds. Your Honours, so that the record is clear, the original documentary contains the interview of General Milovanovic interwoven with other material. The Prosecutor considered -- the Prosecution considered that editing out the short pieces of material between General Milovanovic's comments would have made the clip incomprehensible. The Prosecution only relies on the comments of General Milovanovic. Of course, if the Chamber wants us to edit out these short passages, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, General, I would ask you now to please watch and listen to 65 ter 2609.2, clip number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Manojlo Milovanovic: I arrived there on 12 February 1995, on orders from General Mladic. He had conveyed to me that this was the stance of both the Yugoslav Supreme Defence Council and our own Supreme Command, that I should take over command of Operation Spider. "Narrator: While waiting for the hand-over of duties, Milovanovic inspected the front line. The initial skirmishes between Abdic's Territorial Defence and the 5th Corps soon turned into exceptionally vicious fighting. In fact, the bloodiest combat unfolded between the Muslims themselves. "Manojlo Milovanovic: I watched those soldiers of Fikret's. They fought like mad. I watched a platoon in attack, it was dreadful. Their number was halved by the men of the 5th Corps, yet they continued crawling, pushing some concrete construction blocks in front of them. They tried rolling those blocks, their fingers flying off. "Atif Dudakovic: According to some figures, as many as 1.700 of Abdic's soldiers were killed in the fighting against the 5th Corps, while 1.300 of Abdic's soldiers were killed in fighting against the Serbian Krajina army. This shows that in terms of intensity the fighting between the 5th Corps and Abdic's forces was more severe. "Narrator: Legija and Rajo Bozovic, whose code-name on this occasion was Kobac, would take their orders only from Frenki. "Manojlo Milovanovic: Frenki then arrived accompanied by another man who also wore a red beret and blue uniform. I believe his name was Bozovic and that he held a rank of colonel. They didn't stay long because things were, as one would say, really hot. We only greeted each other. I asked Frenki, as I had heard about him but had never seen him before, 'What are you doing here?' He replied, 'Jovica Stanisic has come, and I have come with him.' "Narrator: Even so, Milovanovic never became the commander of Operation Spider. "Manojlo Milovanovic: Not a single general or Yugoslav army officer who would carry out the rotation, replace General Novakovic and appoint me, came to the meeting. Instead Jovica Stanisic came. I believe he was the chief of the Serbian state security. I told him, 'Jovica, I will not carry out orders from you. You are a policeman not a soldier.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my first question is: The portions of that clip which purport to record what you have said, are they accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the beginning of the clip you refer to the date 12 February 1995, is that the date that you arrived on orders from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not the date. It was on the 22nd of February, 1995, ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the passage you say: "He had conveyed to me that this was the stance of both the Yugoslav Supreme Defence Council" -- I'm sorry, I think I am maybe a bit ahead of myself. Can I ask you to describe in a little more detail your interaction with Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you asked the Presiding Judge for permission to comment on the previous excerpt, I would also seek similar leave to comment so as not to misinform the Chamber much the way it happened at the beginning of the testimony concerning June. Sometime in mid-February 1995, General Mladic was in Belgrade. He phoned me, telling me that I should get ready, and that in a few days I was to travel to a place called Samarice. At first I thought it was Sumarica, where the monument to the Serbs killed near Kragujevac was. I asked him why was I to go to Kragujevac. And he said, "No, not there, you're going to Petrova Gora." I guess the place where a command there was was called Samarice. In any case, he told me, "Most probably you will assume command of Operation Spider. You will remain the Chief of Staff, and upon completion of that task you will return to Han Pijesak." I was familiar with Operation Spider, I knew who was supposed to carry it out and how, and I also knew that as part of the forces of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, there were also Fikret Abdic's forces or the so-called the People's Defence of Western Bosnia. I will discuss that later as well. Five months prior to that, I had refused to co-operate with the People's Defence of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, and at that time I told Mladic, "Boss, I won't command any Muslims, even if they were Abdic's men." He said, "Implement my order because this is an order of the supreme commander, Mr. Karadzic. You are to go to Petrova Gora." I arrived there on the 22nd. When the meeting was supposed to take place, I was told that the entire Supreme Command of the Republic of Srpska Krajina was to attend as well as the commander of our 2nd Krajina Corps, General Tomanic, and that there will be someone from Yugoslavia. When I arrived on the 22nd in the area of Petrova Gora, I was told that the meeting was postponed for the next day, the 23rd. I located General Mile Novakovic, who was in command of Operation Spider. We placed our -- we placed insignia on our sleeves, indicating that we were members of the force of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, so as to be able to move through check-points. Mile wanted to take me to the front line to see -- to show me how those people fought. We -- on the way we went to an observation point where he had a small office and we observed this group in attack referred to in the footage, advancing down a slope. These were Fikret Abdic's men. As we were watching, two men in uniform approached us, one in camouflage military uniform and the other in a police uniform. The one wearing the police uniform had the insignia indicating that he was a colonel. Since I had never seen Frenki in uniform, I asked him who he was, and he said, "I am Frenki." In reply I said, "Oh, so you're the one." The other one introduced himself - I still think it was Bozovic - he spoke with a Montenegrin dialect, and I concluded that he also came from Yugoslavia. When I asked Frenki what he was doing there, he said, "Well, Jovica Stanisic arrived and I came with him." I think the conversation took less than two minutes and we had to move out because the situation got really hot, as I put it in the footage. There was some fierce fighting. The next day I arrived in the place where I was told the meeting was to be held, in a building at Petrova Gora. I didn't know then and I still don't know what the building was used for. A policeman took us to the first floor, into a room where I found Jovica Stanisic. I asked him, "Jovica, why -- what are you doing here?" And he said, "Well, I'm here to attend the meeting." We entered the room, the meeting room, and out of the officers there the most senior person was the Chief of Staff of the Serbian Krajina army, Major-General Dusan Loncar. There were a number of corps commanders whom I recognised, as well as some other officers. In total there were between 40 and 50 men in the meeting room. Jovica told them -- well, yes, Frenki was there. Jovica spoke to them about the disaccord or rifts among the political leadership in -- of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, saying that if they were to go on like that, fighting for power and positions, that they were going to lose the war. Frenki discussed problems, mostly security and political problems in the 18th and 39th Corps of the Serb Krajina army. I think it is the Okucani and Banija Corps. He said that similar things were taking place there and that cargo trucks were being stopped carrying assistance and humanitarian aid for the Republic of Serbian Krajina, stating that the army was stopping them and taking goods. At the end of the meeting Jovica Stanisic said that the duty of the commander or command of Operation Spider was to be taken over by General Milovanovic. I asked Jovica, "On whose decision?" And his answer was, "It was the decision of the staff [as interpreted] of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Yugoslav Supreme Defence Council." I told Jovica that I wasn't going to do that. My explanation was as I've already stated earlier, repeating that I was not going to command any Muslim forces, irrespective of who they belonged to, because if we got lucky and defeated the 5th Corps of Atif Dudakovic, who was to make any guarantees to me that I wasn't going to fight Abdic's army the next day. Second of all, the area of Bihac was not within our sphere of interest of Republika Srpska. At the beginning of the war we -- the borders decided on were supposed to go via Drina, Sava, and Neretva rivers. I left the meeting, Jovica followed, trying to persuade me, but it didn't do him any good. In the hallway he opened the doors of a room, stating, "There's a man who wants to see you." I thought it would be an officer of my generation from back at school, but when I got in, I encountered Fikret Abdic. He was seated there on a couch, drinking milk. He seemed to have a cold. That was my first meeting with Fikret Abdic -- actually, on the 8th of November, 1994, I met him for the first time together with Jovica Stanisic, and on that occasion I did not greet him. On this occasion, however, I wanted to appear more civil so I did greet him and we spoke for about three to four minutes, upon which I left the room. Before that, I said good-byes to Jovica Stanisic and returned to the Main Staff. No one ever asked me afterwards why I refused to assume command of Operation Spider.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, if I can just take you back and ask you a specific question about what you have just told us. The transcript at page 28, line 21, records you as saying the follows: "I asked Jovica, 'On whose decision?' And his answer was, 'It was the decision of the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Yugoslav Supreme Defence Council.'" Did the record correctly record what you remember Jovica Stanisic saying to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm positive that he did not say the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He could only have said of the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska. As I've said at the beginning of my testimony on this issue, General Mladic phoned me from Belgrade to get ready to travel, hence the Main Staff did not sit and discuss this. General Mladic also left the decision to me. He didn't decide that I should assume that duty. Had he done so, I would have obeyed his order --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, just before we get too far away from it, since there is some confusion, it appears, can I ask you to say again, as accurately as you're able, what precisely did Jovica Stanisic say to you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked Jovica on whose orders he was to convey it to me. He said, "Based on the decision of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY and the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska." On the table in front of him there was a piece of paper. He indicated the name of Slobodan Milosevic with a pencil in his hand. It was towards the bottom of the page. I don't know what the paper actually contained and whether it was an order or not, but I only know that since he indicated the name to me, I assumed he didn't want anyone else to hear his name mentioned. And I told him, "Only Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic could issue orders to me, not this person."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we usually have sessions of 75 minutes. It's quarter past 10.00. Could you find a suitable moment, whether that would be now or within the next five minutes, to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This would be suitable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be a suitable moment. Then we'll have a break and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, there's a great volume of other material I want to ask you questions about today. I'm concerned about the time, so I'm going to play the remaining clips from the documentary. This next clip, I won't ask for any extensive comment on. I would just ask you whether it's accurate and truthful. If we have time at the end of your testimony or at the end of this examination, I will come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Laugel play the next clip, 65 ter 2609.2, clip number 2 from this video. It is approximately one minute in duration and is found in the original complete documentary beginning at 36 minutes, 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Manojlo Milovanovic: Sometime in the evening, I received a call from a Drina Corps colonel. His name was Svetozar Andric. Furious and revolted, he said: 'General, can anybody be allowed to beat Serbian officers?' Not knowing what it was about, I replied: 'They can. The Muslims beat us every time they get a chance to.' But he said: 'I was just beaten up by Arkan.' I asked him: "Where?' He said: 'In Prijedor.' 'What was Arkan doing there?' I asked. Andric replied: 'I don't know.' "Colonel, Former VRS Brigade Commander: He simply arrested one of the officers of my brigade, in the area between Sanski Most and Prijedor. Arkan didn't arrest him; he intercepted him like a criminal on the road, took his vehicle, and shaved the man's head. Arkan abused him for a completely incomprehensible reason: The man didn't hold a pass issued by Arkan. "Manojlo Milanovic: 'They intercepted me and beat me,' said the man as he returned from the front, I don't know where. He said: 'They beat me. He, himself, beat me.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the sake of a clear record, the passage -- there was another person speaking in the middle of that who was not identified. The text that he began his intervention was: "He simply arrested," and it ended with "pass issued by Arkan." The remainder of that was Colonel -- or General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, is that passage -- is your portion or the portion that you speak in that passage truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is there any way that we could get a time-frame for the events the witness was talking about in this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you orient us as to time and location with respect to what you are referring to in this videotape?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was approximately in early September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask Mr. Laugel to play 65 ter number 2609.2, clip 3. This clip is found at 38 minutes, 35 seconds, to 40 minutes, 2 seconds of the original and complete documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Manojlo Milovanovic: I asked: 'On whose order did you come here? How did you get here in the first place?' He replied: 'I came here on President Karadzic's order.' Karadzic was present, sitting opposite me, but Karadzic kept quiet and so did Krajisnik. Karadzic was fiddling his fingers like a child who had done something wrong. 'Let me see that order!' Arkan replied: 'I left it at the hotel.' 'Mr. President, does Arkan have your order to come here?' Karadzic failed to say either 'yes' or 'no,' and he remained silent. "At that point Arkan started talking hot air, saying how hard it was for him to leave his 22-year-old wife behind him who was pining after him. He had just married Ceca. I said: 'What do I care about your 22-year-old wife?' Mladic and I had already agreed on how to get rid of Arkan. I said: 'I will be going to Manjaca this evening to drive out your remaining soldiers, while Mladic will do the same in Kotorski, as he has set off for Han Pijesak. In 24 hours' time, there will be no trace of you here!'"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, again, is this truthful and accurate, the information that you provided in this documentary?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, you refer to specific plans to expel Arkan at this period. And first maybe if I could ask you, could you orient us again as to -- as to time-period that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in late September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it appears from what your -- your comments that there were specific plans to expel Arkan at that time. And my question to you is: Were you able or did you have an estimate of how many of Arkan's fighters were in the area controlled by the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have precise information. I only know -- I only knew that Arkan was there with a group of fighters. I don't think it was the whole brigade, though, but I cannot tell you anything precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then the other question that I have with respect to your -- this particular clip, there's a reference to an order. Did you ever see that written order? Was it ever brought for you to see?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was never shown it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have concluded my questions arising out of General Milovanovic's interview in the second part of the documentary "The Unit." At this time I would tender 2609.2 into evidence. It is comprised of the three clips bearing the time codes previously mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P377, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P377 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, after you arrived at the Tribunal, were you asked to review a number of official documents of the Army of Republika Srpska and give your opinion as to whether the documents were authentic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to now ask you a series of questions related to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Milovanovic has been quite resolute in expressing his strong wish that all of his testimony be heard in public session, but I want to ask him about documents which are presently subject to some restriction and must be discussed in private session. Could I ask that we move into private session briefly to discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- this set of documents relates to the newly acquired diaries and other documents that have been seized and provided by the Government of Serbia. I do believe we can deal with this matter entirely in public if we do two things. One, that the chart that General Milovanovic filled out is not displayed on the monitor; and two, that General Milovanovic not say who he recognises the author of these books, but to simply states that he has recorded that fact on the sheet that we are looking at on our screens. In addition to allowing as much of these proceedings to proceed in public as possible, there is the added benefit to taking this evidence -- there is an added benefit to taking this evidence in public session. It is likely that these books will be relevant in several trials before the Tribunal. This limited portion of General Milovanovic's evidence, if given publicly, may be used by Prosecution and Defence teams in other cases to establish the authenticity of these books without having to seek variations of protective measures from this Chamber. It will also serve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the reason why Mr. Weber had not switched off his telephone are known by the Chamber, and the Chamber has accepted it. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It will also serve as -- it will also make it possible for other Defence teams to be on notice about General Milovanovic's testimony once any possible motion by the Government of Serbia is filed and decided by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Milovanovic, the Chamber appreciates that you insist on giving your testimony in public. At the same time, this Tribunal sometimes engages in obligations towards the parties that provide certain documents, and here this is not public knowledge. Therefore, you should not speak with anyone about it. It is the Republic of Serbia who has requested that these documents, at least at this moment, will not be dealt with in public session or at least not to reveal the documents in public session. May I take it that if this is the reason why we would hear either your testimony in closed session or hear your testimony in such a way that the documents will not be identified, if you would testify in public session that you have no problems in meeting in this way the request by the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, Your Honour, I'm here because I was summoned to appear before you. And it is certainly in my interest as well to meet the request of the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I hear from the Defence whether the proposed course to be taken meets any objection. And I am inclined, but let me just check with my colleagues ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has some preference for hearing your testimony also in this respect in open session, but then in such a way that we'll not specifically refer to what the documents exactly are apart from that we can see it on our screens. And I take it then that the charts would be sought to be admitted into evidence and that they'll be confidential exhibits. Further, if it comes to books, I would even speak in a more neutral way about documents because people might ask themselves why we are suddenly talking about books and what those books are. And therefore, I would just refer to exhibits or give the 65 ter numbers rather than to refer to what we know are books but which might give a clue to what the material really is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before we go back into public session, if I can just take this advantage of the opportunity to avoid confusion later on in the examination, I will ask the General to deal with two diaries of General Mladic that there are no request for protective measures and they have been used publicly in other trials, so not to be alarmed when I, all of a sudden, start talking about such diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I must admit that I do not follow in every detail what happens in every trials, not because I'm not interested but because I just don't find the time. Then, Mr. Milovanovic, please carefully listen to the way in which Mr. Groome will phrase his question and avoid in answering that the documents which are provided to the Tribunal as confidential documents at this moment, that your answers will not be such that the public could identify what these documents are. If you think that you couldn't answer the question in such a way, then please ask us to go into private session for a moment so that you can speak freely if there's any need to include in your answer any clue to the -- what the documents exactly are. What you see on your screen then will not be shown to the public. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I did not ask you any questions while we were in private session, and with the Court's permission, we will proceed cautiously in public session. So I would ask you to give me short, precise answers to the questions I'm about to ask you. The first question is: Were you asked to look at a series of 18 documents after you arrived here in Holland? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you told who the author of these documents was prior to being allowed to see them? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not told, but I concluded that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you provided any information regarding where the documents came from? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without mentioning any names, did you recognise the handwriting of the person who wrote in these documents, the person or persons who wrote in these documents? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask at this time that document number 5287 be brought to the screens before us and that it not be displayed to the public. It is a chart containing the notations made by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for the English, if I can ask you, do you recognise the document that you see on the left-hand side of the screen? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this where you recorded the identity of the person whose handwriting you recognised -- the person or persons whose handwriting you recognised on the document that is now before us? I'm sorry, let me rephrase that. The document that we're looking at, is this where you recorded the identity of the person or persons whose handwriting you recognise when you reviewed the 18 documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a two-page document. Did you -- can I ask you, did you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the second page, could I ask you, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of the notes you made on the chart that we now have before us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe the second page now is coming up before you, and I ask you, do you see your signature on the second page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the wrong document. Your Honour, there may be a problem. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that we have the English version before us for the second page, whereas for the other -- for the first page -- we have the English version of the second page before us. For the first page, the signature was on the original, not on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Laugel -- we're looking at it on our monitor. I'm not technically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check what we have in the original. Yes, the original version has ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, do you see your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that the document on the screen be marked for identification, and given the sensitivity, although the public usually doesn't have access to exhibits marked for identification, maybe that we note that it be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before we do so let me just try to understand what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I might be able to enlighten the Chamber as to the handwritten notes on the bottom if that's the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm first of all interested in the -- I see that in the fourth column names appear. Now, what the fourth column stands for, you wouldn't expect the names we see there; you would rather expect that to be in the fifth column, as we find it on the first page. But if that's explained in the handwriting, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour. And perhaps the best way to deal with this if we could have an image of that on the screen, I will ask the witness to make -- if he needs to make any corrections and we can save a copy, an edited copy that he does right here in court. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I briefly ask the witness. Mr. Milovanovic, I see that on the first page of this document you have initialled the third column. Consistently you have made some changes to the ERN numbers. Then the third column -- the fourth column is on the first page empty. And then in the fifth column names appear. Now, on the second page, again your initials appear in the third column, then names which we find on the first page in the fifth column here now appear in the fourth column, which seems to be a bit illogical if you look at the heading of that fourth column. Was it your intention to write down the names we now find in the fourth column, to write them down in the fifth column, as you did on the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, so this is just a technical error. The first page was shown to me how this was done. I guess the second page wasn't. I think the people who were working with me thought that I would be bright enough to get it, but I actually wrote it in the wrong column. So everything that's in the fourth column should be entered in the fifth column and the fourth column should be blank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is now clear. Then we perhaps now move on to the handwriting at the bottom. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court will accept my representation until the English translation is done, but there were some documents contained in -- among the documents that General Milovanovic did not recognise the handwriting and he simply noted the ERN number of those documents. And the last one, Your Honour, is just an explanation that he did not have sufficient time to study the documents in order to adequately fill out column 6 and that's why column 6 has been left blank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With these clarifications, is there any objection to admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I -- because I have not made a motion to actually introduce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I thought it more appropriate to leave it as marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just raise one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was wondering if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, as you are aware of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. When the witness was asked whether he was provided with any information regarding where the documents came from, he answered "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would like to know what he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we should move for that purpose into private session in order to avoid any risk. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness, when you said that you were provided with information as to where these documents came from, could you tell us what the information was you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak with the open text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that you have the text on your screen or that we are -- at this moment the public will not hear your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can say what the Prosecutor told me while preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told that the documents were received from the Government of the Republic of Serbia and that this is something that I should keep confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was anything else told you -- told to you as -- were any further details given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just explained to me how I should fill in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, for example, you were not told where they had been found, in archives, or whether that was in Banja Luka or Belgrade or Zagreb or -- were you given any further details as to the origin of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, does this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- sufficiently deal with the matter? Then we move into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Usually I do not ask whether there's any objection for documents to be marked for identification because they are not then admitted into evidence. At the same time, if a document is marked for identification, then certainly the answers given to questions may have some evidentiary value. No objections. Madam Registrar, the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P378, marked for identification, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will keep that status, under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that document number 5288 be displayed on the screen. It is a two-page document containing both typed and handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this one can be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just pause because I'm not sure that we have the English translation yet. It was just done last night, but I suppose we'll see in the next minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for that to come up, were you also asked to review a binder of 11 documents originating from the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was shown a number of binders yesterday, so I'm not sure exactly which one you're thinking of. There were some with 11, less, more, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The one I'm asking you about now is the binder with 11 documents, and your notes regarding that are now on the screen before you. So maybe if you take a look at that, and I ask you, does that refresh your recollection as to which specific binder you were asked to look at.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you review these documents and form an opinion with respect to whether the documents are copies of authentic documents originating from the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the documents that were reviewed were copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And based upon your review of these copies, were you able to form an opinion or an assessment as to whether they were copies of authentic documents of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That should be entered in the review. If a document was authentic, I would put yes; and if not, I would enter a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what we're looking at before you, is this the document upon which you recorded your assessment of these 11 documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could zoom out a little bit, it might be easier for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. Every document has my initials with a brief comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the second page, did you record these comments in the right-hand column of this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is in column 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is the document that we're looking at a fair and accurate representation of the comments that you recorded yesterday when you reviewed these 11 documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I see my handwriting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I notice that in the English version initials which are asked for in columns 5 and 6 are not present, whereas they seem to be present in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I could address that and then I would ask that it be marked for identification at this point in time and I'll have the translation unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then provide for at least the full English version. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution does ask that this be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the parties have seen that the English version is not complete because some of the handwriting is missing. Furthermore, where it says "Signature," the -- a reference to a signature is missing at the bottom of the document, whereas in the original we see that there is a signature in blue handwriting. Any objections? Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number for this document to be marked for identification.
