utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P379, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It will keep that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, do I correctly summarise your assessment of the authenticity of these documents when I say the following, that you found that all of them were authentic with the exception of document number 4 on the list, and for that document you did not believe that you were able to make an assessment of the authenticity of that document. Have I correctly stated your conclusions with respect to these 11 documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'm going to tender the exhibits referenced here, with the exception of number 4, which is 65 ter 94. And, Your Honour, taking the point that the Chamber has made on several occasions, the Chamber is able to read documents that are clear on their face for themselves. Given that each of these ten documents speaks for itself and given the unique situation in which General Milovanovic has refused to be a witness in the case and that he only arrived in The Hague yesterday pursuant to a subpoena, the Prosecution has been unable to determine whether he has any particular knowledge over and above what the documents say on their face. The Prosecution believes it would not necessarily be productive or efficient for me to now ask the General to read each of these documents in your presence and comment. So it is not my intention to do so. I recognise that the right and the interest -- I recognise that the Defence and the Chamber may have an interest in asking questions about these documents, but the Prosecution at this time is content to rest on the simple text of the document and has no additional questions for General Milovanovic. And with that, Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender the ten documents that are identified in this chart and the 65 ter number is included on the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, you summarised what the position of the witness was in relation to the authenticity. While I tried to follow you in respect of document number 7 -- well, the only way of making that an authentic document is -- requires some intellectual gymnastics because I see in the original in the column "Not authentic," a "no." Now, if you take that literally, you could say if the question of being not authentic is answered by no, you could conclude that it is authentic. But that is a kind of gymnastics which I would not -- it is more likely I would say that the witness by writing "ne" denies the authenticity of document number 7. Could you comment on that, Mr. Groome, on what basis you said that it was only in relation to document 4 that the witness denied authenticity and that for all the others he confirmed the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with -- it's my mistake. If I could clarify what it is he has to say with respect to 7, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we can read that, but if you would change your summary in that the witness has denied in respect of documents 4 and 7 -- let me just look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, now that I'm able to see the English translation, I withdraw my tendering of 65 ter 4696. I don't believe that there is proper basis at this time for admission of that document. So I would withdraw my application with respect to items 4 and 7 on this list, that's 65 ter 94 and 65 ter 4696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There are objections to the admission of the documents. We obviously -- well, maybe not obviously, but we accept that the Prosecution have crossed the authenticity threshold, but what the Prosecution have to do, we submit, is then cross the relevance threshold. And because this witness has attended subject to a subpoena does not obviate the need for the Prosecution to explain either through a bar table motion or through a witness the precise relevance and probative value of these documents. If I can just take one particular example to demonstrate the point, Exhibit 105 -- I think it's 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's number 9 on the list, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Is a 165-page document, detailing, as the title suggests, the combat-readiness and the activities of the Republika Srpska in 1992. It cannot be, we submit, that every page of that document is relevant. And it cannot be that, in our submission, that that document can be simply tendered without some explanation as to why the combat-readiness of the VRS is relevant to the charges in this indictment. There are another -- a number of other documents which we have the same precise issue with, which we cannot actually work out what the probative value of the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have two issues here, Mr. Groome, I think identified by Mr. Jordash: Relevance and probative value. That is a question which is not answered just by authenticity. I could provide you with a lot of authentic documents which have no relevance and no probative value. Now, usually if a witness does not give any information as to the content of documents, which he does not here, at least I would have to go through the seventh column in detail before I would know whether we find anything in there. But as Mr. Jordash said, sometimes there are very lengthy documents. We have not heard any evidence on the content of it. It sounds as if we are dealing with bar table documents, where any debate on authenticity is avoided by providing evidence as to the authenticity of these documents, which would lead me to suggest that we deal with these documents as with -- as we usually do with bar table documents, is that we have a chart and that you briefly describe the relevance for what portions of the -- what portions of the indictment they relate to and any other matter, which is what to focus on. For example, if we have a very lengthy document, the Chamber is invited to look at page so and so and so, so that we know what you are seeking to establish through these documents because the mere fact that they're authentic is fine but doesn't give much guidance for the Chamber as to how to -- what to specifically look at. That we then follow the usual procedure for bar table documents, that the Defence is able to comment on that, and that the Chamber would then receive the chart knowing what the relevance is, where to look in the document, what the comment of the Defence is, so that we with all that information then can decide on admission. Is this -- I'm first looking to you whether that's -- whether you consider this suggestion to be one which is practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution does, Your Honour. So at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll ask the Defence teams whether they would agree. So apart from the authenticity, to deal with these documents as if it were a bar table submission, which would meet, I think, the concerns you have expressed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. During our cross-examination we may ask the witness about some of the documents, which would then obviate the need for the bar table motion. But yes, we agree in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if you start asking questions about the substance of the documents, then of course they lose more or less their character of bar table documents and might well then -- that we have to decide on admission of those specific documents already at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we absolutely agree with your proposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then since the witness has written down his observations as far as authenticity is concerned, I suggest that for the time being that the documents will be bar tabled, but we also could wait -- could be MFI'd, but, of course, we could also wait because in the previously admitted exhibit we have all the relevant information. Although for the other chart, we have chosen for the option that the -- let me see. No, you didn't seek their -- the underlying documents all to be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe I'd have to -- the Prosecution would have to make an application to amend our 65 ter exhibit list, so we would do that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have one concern, that if they're not MFI'd, they do not appear -- it would not appear on our MFI list, and therefore they might get lost somewhere in the further proceedings. So therefore, I would like to -- Madam Registrar, to prepare a list giving the 65 ter numbers, to copy the description of the document, and then on that same list, with the exceptions of the numbers 4 and 7 appearing on this list, to prepare a list in which provisionally numbers will be assigned. And then once we have received that list, we'll MFI those documents under those numbers suggested by Madam Registrar. And then at a later stage, we'll receive or not receive a bar table motion in the format as the Chamber usually requests. Madam Registrar, if you would prepare that, then we'll deal with that at a later stage. Perhaps we could already reserve nine numbers on the list, which will then appear on the further prepared list at a later stage, but that we would leave those numbers for the time being open as being the expected MFI numbers for those nine documents. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that the Court Officer call up 65 ter 5067 on the screen. It is a document dated 21st of February, 1994, and marked "Very urgent." The name of the author is General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, when the document appears on the screen I'm going to ask you whether you recognise it, but I want to preface my remarks by saying it is not -- my focus is not the actual substance of the document, but more the addressees of the document. So if I could ask you to pay attention to the addressees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is this a document which can be shown to the public or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it can. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General Milovanovic, once -- if you indicate us -- to us when you've had a chance to look at this first page, I'll ask the Court Officer to move to the second page so that you can see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can barely read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we enlarge the text so that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you let us know when you need it to be scrolled down so that you can review all of the document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already gone to page 2, but I haven't finished page 1. Very well. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, have you finished reading or reviewing the document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just deal with authenticity first. Do you have an assessment as to whether or not this document is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was written in my style.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, as I said, my primary focus with this document are the addressees. Now, this letter is sent to four addressees: The president of the Republic of Serbia, at that time Slobodan Milosevic; the president of Republika Srpska, at that time Radovan Karadzic; the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army, at that time General Perisic; and finally the state security department of the MUP of Serbia, at that time headed by Jovica Stanisic. Can I ask why was this document sent to President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in mind President Milosevic or General Milosevic? There's two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could tell us the -- the first addressee, is it not the president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, to the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic. I was inquiring about the identity because there was a general by the name of Slobodan Milosevic, however, in the Army of Republika Srpska. This is an authentic document. I drafted it based on the documents referred therein. And what would be your question about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question is: Why was the document sent to President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is why. Firstly, the area of Bihac, the so-called Cazina Krajina was unilaterally by the Security Council of the UN in May of 1993, almost a year before this, was declared a safe area. In that area, according to that Security Council Resolution, there should have been no arms, no armed force. The 5th Corps had to be disarmed; however, instead of disarming the 5th Corps, UNPROFOR informed us -- they did tell us that the 5th Corps was disarmed and that its three brigades were disbanded. That's what it -- their report stated. However, in October 1993, a Territorial Defence was formed. It was formed somewhat before that but made official in October 1993. That was the Territorial Defence of the autonomous area of Western Bosnia. This was a new eighth armed force in the territory of the former SFRY. In this report mention is made of the arming of the 5th Corps, which is done with the assistance of UNPROFOR, which was there to disarm them in the first place, as well as the arming of the armed force of Fikret Abdic which developed through the channels of the Army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. All of these conducted themselves in contravention to the Security Council Resolution. General Mladic was probably not at the command post at that point in time, and I, as his deputy, found it necessary to inform of this the president of Serbia because in October, he was a signatory to a peace agreement with Fikret Abdic, as well as to the president of Republika Srpska, with whom I had arguments about that peace declaration, I think that's what it was called, which he also signed with Fikret Abdic. And I also sent it to the Chief of the General Staff of our neighbouring armed force as well as to the MUP of Serbia, because the police were those who were to -- supposed to prevent any illegal weapons transport. Simply said, the embargo on weapons was violated, which was also one of the provisions of that Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, were there types of documents generated by the Army of Republika Srpska that were routinely sent to the state security department of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the number you can see in the heading, strictly confidential 18/19. In any case, the figure of 18 indicates that this was done by the security organ at the staff. Mladic's number was 01, mine 02, Gvero 04, and the operational department had 03. Number 18 is someone from the security, and I signed it probably as the most senior officer at the command post. It is possible that I drafted it because this would be my writing style. I don't see anything questionable about this. Any security service and security intelligence organs of one country inform all security organs of their neighbouring countries if there are on -- on friendly terms. This is the usual intelligence type co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 5067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P389, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P389 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 4505 on the screens before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for this, 65 ter 4505 is a photograph depicting four men standing next to each other. After it appears on the screen before you, I'm going to ask you to identify each person in the photograph, and would you please do this starting with the person on the left-hand side of the photograph in a suit and work your way to the person standing on the right-hand side of the photograph in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first, in front of the flags, is Momcilo Krajisnik; next to him, Jovica Stanisic. The person with the bundle of hair is Radovan Karadzic. In uniform -- well, I can't make this person out so well today, but I think yesterday it was clear to me that this was Frenki, the person with the glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we zoom out so that we can see the entire picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you, General, do you recognise the location, or by some of the items that we see in the photograph, do you have some idea about the possible location?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recognise the setting, but the photograph must have been taken somewhere in Serbia. I conclude that based on the three flags in the background. The first two ones to the right, immediately behind Krajisnik, were the republican or state flags. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time in its more important offices had the flags of the FRY, the flag of Serbia, and the third is the flag of an institution or a ministry, wherever they were. In Republika Srpska at the time, in such locations, one would not come across three but two flags instead: The flag of Republika Srpska and the flag of an institution or a ministry. And the coat of arms between the heads of Radovan Karadzic and Frenki does not resemble the coat of arms of Republika Srpska. We also have a two-headed eagle, but it is white. Of course, I also take into account that this was taken during the war, and I base that conclusion because of Krajisnik's and Karadzic's hair look. That was his hairstyle during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 65 ter 4505 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P390 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock. We have sessions of 75 minutes usually, which would be -- let me just see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we have now done for 75 minutes. In totality we are a little bit under two and a half hours. If we would have a break now, how much time would you still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually impossible for me to estimate because -- I'll explain what I have left, Your Honour. I want to show the witness one more photograph and then several entries from a diary of General Mladic that I believe are highly probative. But not having had the opportunity to ask the witness what he knows about these diary entries, it's impossible for me to say. I have, I believe, seven entries. Some of them, I think, speak for themselves, and I will not ask questions other than to ask his opinion about the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you make a calculated guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would think one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we would not finish your examination-in-chief anyhow because there are some charts still outstanding, isn't it, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to ask for 15 minutes on Wednesday if -- after I fully explain my proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 12.30. I'm also keeping in mind, of course, the total of time Mr. Stanisic is usually attending court. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Would the Court Officer please display 65 ter 4494 on the screens before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, when this -- this is a photograph depicting seven men, and it will take a minute to bring it to the screen. Six of the men are sitting. After the picture appears on the screen before you, would you please identify the six men sitting down, starting on the left-hand side of the photograph and moving to the right-hand side of the photograph. I will ask you about the man who is standing after you have told us whether you recognise the first six men.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I please stand up because at this angle I can't see too well. I can see it much better now. The first to the left, with the beard, is Stojan Zupljanin. The second resembles Frenki, although I'm not positive, since I have never seen him in civilian clothes. Next is Momcilo Krajisnik, and Jovica Stanisic, Radovan Karadzic. Milan Martic is the last person seated. And behind him is Dragan Kijac, standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can you tell us who Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Kijac for a while was the interior minister of the RS towards the end of the war, I think, or -- and the first war immediately following the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I think it's the first time during this trial that Stojan Zupljanin's name has been mentioned. Can you tell us if you know what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin, I saw him only once during the war. He was the chief of the state security sector in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the location where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can only see the curtains and it doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Judging by the appearance of the men in the photograph, are you able to estimate when the photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Everyone seems very relaxed and in good spirit. There are no worried faces to be seen. However, it was probably taken during the war because Milan Martic is there. He was the then-president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Perhaps it was towards the end of the war because we also have Kijac appearing. Karadzic's and Krajisnik's hairstyle is unchanged. Zupljanin -- well, when I saw him in the middle of the war, he had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 65 ter 4494.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I inquire from the Prosecution as to where the photograph came from, where they received it from. That might clarify some of the issues that my learned friend was just asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to check this, but I believe it was given confidentially to the chief of investigations of the Tribunal. I'm not sure if the Chamber wishes more information, I'll explore it over the weekend and have more information Wednesday. But the information I know is very limited about where we received this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you -- I take it that Mr. Groome will further inform us. Is it an objection to admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it's not an objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from the Simatovic Defence. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P391 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now ask that 65 ter 5053 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. You said it was given confidentially. Does that require any further status as to whether it's a public document or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My understanding is that the person wished not to be identified, not that the photograph itself needed to be confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now I understand, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 5053.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while that's being displayed and oriented on our screens, can I ask you, were senior officers in the Army of Republika Srpska required to keep diaries or journals of their professional activities?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Such a thing was not ordered specifically, but this is the training we had received in military schools, that we were supposed to keep notes in notebooks such as the one that we can see the cover page of. There was a bigger one used by the more senior officers who moved about in the field, and there was a notebook half the size which could be carried around in your pocket. Every officer would be issued with one. There were no regulations dictating what notes should be kept, but one was free to record everything done during the day, such as orders received, issued, descriptions of events. Well, we did basically anyone else would have in terms of keeping notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could -- would -- would an officer or could an officer be required by his or her superior to produce the book for review?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Each officer had a notebook. They would be issued with one. And when you opened it, on the cover page you would probably find the following text: Notebook, working notebook, then the officer's first and last name, a registry number, and when the notebook is used up it is supposed to be returned to the office issuing it. There were no specific orders in terms of production of such notebooks and requirements for review. However, if I needed some information, I would inquire of the relevant officer and they would probably consult their notebooks to remind themselves. But there was no particular obligation on the part of the subordinate to report on what he had entered. I usually wrote down the things I thought were important or because I was afraid I would forget them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now we are looking at on the screen now excerpt number 1 of 65 ter 5053.1. You've already described that we're looking at the cover of these books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So could I ask the Court Officer to please proceed to excerpt 2 of 5053.1. And it is -- in the English translation it's page 51 or in the original ERN -- the original the ERN ends in 0175. I'm sorry, I misspoke. It's page 37 in the English translation. So the ERN ending 0175 and the English translation page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, when I'm -- when this is brought to the screen, I'm going to ask you to take a look at the handwriting. Please advise us if you need us to make it larger or to do -- change it or re-orient it. And my question to you will be whether you recognise the handwriting. General, while we're sorting out a technical problem, if I could proceed and ask you a few other questions. You've mentioned General Ratko Mladic a number of times in your testimony. My question to you is: For what period of time have you known General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known General Mladic since April 1981. We met in the Titov Veles garrison in Macedonia, and from that time on we became close associates until 1992, until we both came to the front. We spent the whole war together. The last time we saw each other was on the 4th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did you ever have occasion to see General Mladic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us some approximation at the frequency with which you would see his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the first time that we saw each other, then every day, especially during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to be present at a meeting and observe General Mladic make notes in a diary during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all did that regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was his practice to make notes as the different participants in a meeting spoke or to wait until a meeting had ended?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he was not speaking, he was constantly writing down -- writing down what the others were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to read a document immediately after observing General Mladic write that document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because General Mladic, especially during the war, when he was looking at the mail and he would receive some document that would perhaps be for me to deal with, then at the top he would write "chief" or "general," or however he would address me, "do such and such a thing." Usually -- I have to -- I'm sorry, I have to get up because the angle is a little bit awkward. But at the top, for example, it says the day and the date, also the same thing would be written on a typewritten document. He would write: "Chief, do such and such a thing." That would be written on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at whether the angle of the screen could be adjusted for the witness. It's usually rather easy to -- Madam Usher, is there any way that you could just -- if I change this one, it just goes like that. That's not a -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, we're trying to adjust the monitor so you don't have to stand up every time. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's fine. It's fine. Thank you. I don't want to create any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is important that you have a clear image of it, so please do not hesitate to let us know if we need to do something else to make that possible. General, before I ask you about the substance of this particular entry, do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to number 2, the paragraph number 2, and to the particular point that says: "... has permission from Stanisic to form the Red Berets at Ozren ..." Do you know or are you able to tell us who Stanisic refers to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't see that here. I don't see what you've just read out. I can see under 2: "Lazarevic, Slavko, a.k.a. Amerika."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please keep reading that and maybe -- I'm not sure whether we're trimming off the right-hand portion of the document, but we're both in the same paragraph. I was a few -- I was one line ahead of you. So if you continue reading that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Lazarevic Slavko, a.k.a., Amerika, now called Duganovic or Diganovic, lives in Belgrade and has permission from Stanisic to form the Red Berets at Ozren (Mico wrote an order for Bozovic [as interpreted] to form a special unit at the public security centre in Doboj, and these units would" -- I can't read this word. "For CSB in Doboj and these units would" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're unable to read it, that's -- you are unable to read --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not capable of reading it, but this Stanisic in the parenthesis it says, "Mico wrote an order for Boskovic," I think it's Mico Stanisic who for a while was the minister of internal affairs of Republika Srpska. So this is not Jovica Stanisic, I think, but Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your belief that the first Stanisic that's mentioned, "has permission from Stanisic to form the Red Berets," is it your evidence that you believe that that is Mico Stanisic that is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Only his name is mentioned. I don't think that Mladic would have left that. We all would emphasise the name when talking about Jovica Stanisic, we would all make sure that that was there because it was a person from another state. I think it's Mico Stanisic because Jovica Stanisic would not have been able to write an order for the unit to be located in Doboj, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, in the -- the problem with the monitor, I -- we skipped an answer to a question. My question to you when we first looked at this was whether you recognised the handwriting of the person who wrote it. Just so the record is clear, can I ask you that again?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't answer because I didn't know whether it was okay for me to mention the name. Can I mention the name of the person whose handwriting this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, you can, if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would now ask that we look at the last entry in this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 5053.1, excerpt number 3. This begins on page 153 or 155 as the diary is internally numbered or with the ERN ending 0277 and starts on page 139 in the English translation, and it continues for two pages. General, after you've had an opportunity to study the handwriting, I would again ask you: Do you recognise the author of this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It looks like it was written on the knee, on the lap, but it is still Ratko Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the portion or the entry that I'm interested in is recounting a meeting at Tara on the 28th of February, 1993. Am I correct in saying that's at the bottom half of the diary entry? Can you see the entry for a meeting at Tara?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the heading: "Planning of actions." And then there is an abbreviation, JSO, I don't know what that means. Present Panic; Ojdanic, he was the commander of the Uzice Corps at the time; Loncar; I don't know the following name, I can't read it; then Frenki; and two from -- Frenki and two from the MUP, from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, but it doesn't state who. In certain sectors the units -- actually, the units are in certain regions or garrisons for Osmace, Jadar, Kragivode, go with -- and there is an abbreviation there, PO, I don't know what that means, and for Kragivode, and I can't read any further -- actually, there is no more text.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders these three excerpts from 65 ter 5053. They have been extracted from the entire diary and combined as a single exhibit now referred to as 65 ter 5053.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? If not, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, would you please perhaps submit the translation again because it seems that the word processor has taken those who -- the name Loncar appears as "Loncararticle," which sounds a bit odd and is not in conformity with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it also seems, Your Honour, just so that the record is clear, that General Milovanovic has referred to operation planning with JSO and the translation seems to be Udar, U-d-a-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whatever it is. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. I just wanted to mention what my learned friend Mr. Groome mentioned. I would perhaps like to have the text enlarged for the General so that he can see what it says below "planning," because it doesn't actually read what he thinks it reads. The letters are kind of smaller. So perhaps it would be easier for the General just to look at an enlarged image of the writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, perhaps now that it is enlarged, can I ask you to take the pen in front of you and circle where you read "JSO."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say "JSO." I said it is written in the Latinic script "JSO," but I don't know what that abbreviation means. I mean, I'm surprised. Mladic constantly writes in the Cyrillic alphabet, so I don't know why he was using the Roman alphabet because the S is written in the Roman alphabet. And this third letter, I don't even know whether that's an O or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let's -- I see that that's between brackets which do not appear in any way, is not reflected in the translation. Is there anything, having closely looked now at the text, does it in any way influence any of the answers you've given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see anything new here that I didn't see the first time I can decipher. Panic is the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. "Ja" is -- "I" is Ratko Mladic. Then there is Ojdanic, Loncar, and then there were two generals. One Loncar was the Chief of Staff of the Army of Serbian Krajina, and the other one was the chief of the East Slavonia Corps. I think that's the 11th Corps. So I don't know which Loncar it is here. The third one I don't know. Then there is this person Kac [phoen], Kac Stevo was the commander of the air force base Ponikve, near Uzice. So I don't know whether he was air force or infantry officer. The units were in certain sectors - garrisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The issue raised -- first of all, the document has been admitted into evidence and, Mr. Petrovic, you're invited to comment on -- give these kind of comments before it is admitted. Apparently the JSO or Udar matter is -- unless you have any reason to believe that the witness could clarify this apart from that he can read what apparently everyone who would speak the language could read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I think would be important is just to ask him to circle the portion that we've been talking about, the Latin script and what he read, and then save that as a separate exhibit. I think that would assist us if there is a question about the ultimate text later, and that's what I would ask him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could you give the -- Madam Usher, could you give the pen to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can the Usher please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Usher -- could you please give the -- one second, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, there is a special pen that if you use that, we can see what you're writing, it shows up on our screens as well, and the Usher is going to assist you with that now. So if you would simply circle the text that you've referred to as being the Latin script which you understood to read "JSO."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, listening to you and I think the lawyer, I have deciphered this word after the word "as part of." This is an abbreviated word for Operation, "Oper." So it's: "Planning actions as part of the Udar Operation." Your Honour, you helped me in deciphering this middle letter. It's not an S, it's a D in the Cyrillic script, and then we have an R. So this is some kind of operation called Udar. I personally know that the operation was planned, but it was not actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this resolves the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I would ask that we tender -- we save this screen image now that it's been created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it seems that it now is fully reflected by the translation. But if you insist. Madam Registrar, a number for this marked version of the document would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P393 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to work with a different diary at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask the Court Officer to bring to the screen 65 ter 5016.1. It is a series of diary entries extracted from 65 ter 5016.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we are going to see the first page and there is insufficient amount of text in this page to ask you about the handwriting. I simply want to note for the Court that the first page of this book bears the name Kertes and two six-digit numbers. And if I could ask your assistance, General, during the conflict how many digits were in a telephone number?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in the Main Staff we had land-line communications with the Belgrade dialling code in our staff in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We never wrote in the Belgrade area code 011. At the time Belgrade had six-digit telephone numbers. I think after the war some seven-digit telephone numbers were introduced, but at the time there were only six-digit telephone numbers. So these numbers could have been both in Serbia or Republika Srpska. We actually had 31 channels with Belgrade numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So given that there is nothing preceding the six digits, does that lead you to a conclusion as to whether this is a Belgrade number or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this would be a Belgrade number, and this name Kertes, we know or it's known who this person by the name of Kertes was. I think he was the director of the customs administration of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us his full name?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, just the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that we proceed to 65 ter 5016.1 excerpt number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could we ask what a T or a K would stand for in relation to a telephone number, if it is a telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, are you able to assist us with what the T or the K means?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The T, I don't know what that stands for. The K would refer to "kuca," home number. People would always take two numbers. One would be the work number and the other one -- I don't know how that would be indicated. And K would for stand for "kuca," home, so if he wasn't at work they would look at him at home, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now proceed to excerpt 2. It is found in the original at page ending 0375, and in the English translation at page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, in the interests of time, I'm simply going to ask you to study the document until you can make a reliable identification of the handwriting and simply tell us if you recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a little bit, please, on the bottom part of the page. I don't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, the diary entry is rather explicit, so it -- there may not be a need for you to comment on the substance, but are you able to identify the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mladic's handwriting, and what he is writing here is intended for General Djukic and his assistant for logistics. He is informing him here what and how much assistance is being given to him and by whom. They were referring to some 40 million bullets from the Partizan factory. They're referring to some money from the government, from this and that. So it's some sort of a donation here. There is a Trbic, some oil man probably, who gave some 200 tonnes of oil to Republika Srpska, to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I could ask that we move to excerpt number 3 of 65 ter 5016.1. It's a two-page entry that begins in the original on page ending 0375 and page 72 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we are orienting that on the screen before you, could you tell us what the word "Pretis" stands for, p-r-e-t-i-s.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pretis is our ammunitions factory in Sarajevo. It was in Vogosca until the end of the war. After the Dayton Accords it was evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, do you have or can you make an assessment as to whether you recognise the handwriting in this entry?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The bottom part, this bottom part where it says "meeting with General Perisic and Jovica Stanisic, present" -- once again Perisic, Stanisic, Gvero, and myself. Again, this is Mladic's handwriting. At the top this resembles Mladic's "rukopis" but it seems to be written at an angle somewhat so I couldn't really swear that it was Mladic's handwriting. But probably it is because it is on the same page, same kind of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, so that we're certain, the portion of the diary entry that is below the date of 6 April 1995 is the portion of this page that you are certain is the handwriting of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure about the top part also. Only the pen is different, that's why I was confused. He used black ink at the top and blue ink at the bottom. And I cannot read at the top to whom the -- this was sent. Or maybe he was just writing a reminder for himself to emphasise -- what to emphasise, "istaci," at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the second page of this excerpt, and the portion of this that I would draw your attention to is there is an asterisk or star with a double underline. Are you able to read the very top line of this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Jovica Stanisic" is underlined and it's -- has an asterisk next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to read the diary, and you can read it to yourself. We have a translation. But the question that I'm interested in asking you is: Given what you know of General Mladic and working with him, would you -- is the text that we see below "J. Stanisic" that's double underlined, is that -- do you believe that to be a recording of what J. Stanisic said at this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand. Are you asking me whether what Mladic noted down was uttered by Jovica Stanisic or was it something Mladic told Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking you the first version of what you've said. Is what's underneath Stanisic's name what Stanisic said? If you're able to tell.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. See, the asterisk and the double line, this would indicate that Mladic wanted to pay particular attention to that part of the text. However, the asterisk could indicate that this was something Mladic had drafted in order to share with Stanisic. But it could also be the other way around, and then Mladic underlined it to keep it in mind when later on leafing through the notebook. In any case, for some reason he believed this part of the text to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the very last line in this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, I would ask you to read this line out loud to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "To have more freedom to act" and then the last word begins with t-r-a but I can't make out the rest. I can circle it if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe that's necessary at the moment, but my question to you is: Are you able to assist us in what this might be referring to or place it in the context of what was happening around the 6th of April, 1995, when this entry was made?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. I was focusing on something else. I was reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is: Can you help us understand what is intended by that last line or place it in the context of what was occurring in the 6th of April, 1995, the day this entry was made?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is something else I just realised. Jovica Stanisic said this to Mladic and Mladic noted it down because in the fifth line from the top it says: "I sent 150 men from Slavonia as part of Pauk." I don't know what Pauk refers to. I don't think it's Operation Spider that we discussed today because it's not at the same time, but Mladic could not have told Stanisic that he had sent 150 men from Slavonia because Mladic did not have any men in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does -- so am I correct in that your interpretation is that where you said "to have more freedom to act," that you believe that this is Mladic recording the statement of Mr. Stanisic; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there's a confusion, and I'd like to clarify that. Mr. Milovanovic, you're asked a question and then you said: "There is something else I just realised. Jovica Stanisic said this to Mladic ..." Now, did I understand you well that where you had been reading the content of it, that it suddenly came to your mind that what was recorded, not on the last line but on the lines above, that this must have been what Mr. Stanisic would have said to General Mladic rather than the other way around? Or was it an answer specifically in relation to the last line of this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not specifically in relation to the last line. At the beginning I said that I was uncertain whether it was Mladic who had noted down what he was going to tell Stanisic or whether he wrote down what Stanisic told him. And then I realised that because of the mention of 150 men from Slavonia, it could've been [as interpreted] Mladic who sent them. And then I realised that Stanisic said that to Mladic and Mladic wrote it down. As for the "more freedom to act" line, I'm not sure Mladic would suddenly revert to the capitals, but it could have something to do with less control of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, that's how I understood the answer, to be a further reflection on a question you had asked earlier and not specifically an answer to the last line; whereas you, in your next question, interpreted the words of the witness as being an answer to your last question, which I gained -- I had the impression was not and I think that's now -- so if we want to pay attention to the last line you should then re-start that portion of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance in clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, now that you had a chance to think for a few minutes about this entry, can you tell us, do you have a reliable interpretation of that last line, given that it appears to be in capital letters and the text of that line?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already offered my interpretation, to have more freedom to act so that there would be less control and more mutual trust. If there is a vehicle carrying assistance from Serbia via Republika Srpska to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, still it is stopped at every check-point, searched, registered, and so on. Mladic simply wanted a more liberal regime so as not to stall things. He simply wanted us to trust each other, to trust the one sending the goods as well as the one receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From that answer do I take that you don't see that last sentence as a record of what Jovica Stanisic said, but as Mladic recording his own thoughts on restrictions that may have been in effect?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I ask one additional question. Earlier you said that you had difficulties in deciphering the last word of that line. Were you able to decipher that last word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not able. I'm still pondering it. It could be "transparent" or "transport," something of that sort. I'm unable to decipher it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, this requires at least that further attention will be paid to the understanding of this last word, which apparently for those who translated it were able to read, but there seems to be perhaps a little problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, given that the witness before us is probably best equipped to interpret the handwriting and he is unable, I will ask that that be marked illegible in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's first try to find out, first of all, what the persons who appear to be able to read it, what they think the word is. And if then it's on loose grounds that it was translated as it has been translated, then of course it should be declared illegible. But if it's not on loose grounds, then -- but what I wanted -- I want it to be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. If we could proceed to the next excerpt, it's 5016.1, excerpt 4. This is a two-page entry beginning in the original on ERN ending 0457 and in the English on 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, in the interests of time, could I ask you to simply study it until you are able to tell us whether you recognise the handwriting, and we will rely on the plain text of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The handwriting is that of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please move to excerpt number 5 -- I'm sorry, General, you have your -- you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were removing the previous page, perhaps because of the angle or the light, concerning the last line, I think I now know what it means. So to have more freedom to act and then, "- seek a position." Mladic wanted to have a position of probably a state official. So he was trying to remind himself that he was supposed to ask for a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please clarify what you're saying now. He was supposed to ask who for a position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He wrote it down to use it as an aide-memoire, to ask for a position of civilian authorities. He was to propose to those whom he was seeking a position from, that they should be allowed to act more freely. He probably noted it down so as not to forget. I'm positive that the last two words is "seek a position" or "ask for a position." Whether Jovica asked him to have more freedom to act and then Mladic was supposed to ask for a position or something else, that is irrelevant. In any case, it is suggested that more room be provided to act and that a position should be sought. As -- and also most of the text is written in the second-person plural, which would be out of respect. So I conclude it was Jovica Stanisic who was asking him to get a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could now move to excerpt number 5. Again, this is -- ends in ERN 473 and the English translation is on page 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, in the interests of time I'll rely on the plain text, but do you recognise this handwriting as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I believe there may have been a mistake in the transcript. I just want to go back to page 78. It has to do with when you were referring to the 150 men from Slavonia. Were you saying that Mladic could not send 150 men from Slavonia or could send 150 men from Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He could not. We had no men there. It was in the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could now move to excerpt number 6. This is the second-to-last excerpt. It ends in the original 0521, and this is a two-page entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while it's being oriented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked any questions about the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In the interests of time I was going to rely on the plain text of it unless the Chamber -- I'm just conscious of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I better understand why you move to the next excerpt. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My first question again will be: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to focus on the entry recording what is referred to as "talk with President Karadzic" in Pale on the 23rd of June 1995. Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, sorry. No? A discussion with President Milosevic and General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm unable to see the ERN number but it should end with 0521. There seems to be some error in what's up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, there's also a number on the back of this page. I think it's 474.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I further notice that there seems to appear a time in the original at the right top which seems not to be there in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we have the wrong original, so I'm going to see if we can sort that. The ERN number is different than the one I'm calling out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then at least for the one we had on our screen there seems to be a translation issue as well. But I'm not going to insist on that. Let's try to get -- perhaps for those who will ever use this page in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting to see if we can get up the correct entry on the screen, can you tell us where Trnovo is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Trnovo is a small town between Sarajevo and Kalinovik, closer to Sarajevo than to Kalinovik, perhaps some 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now that we have the correct page, can I ask you: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is General Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I draw your attention to the "talk with President Karadzic" in Pale on the 23rd of June, 1995. Let us know when you've read that and I'll ask the Usher to advance to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Conversation with President Karadzic, those in attendance, Toso Tolimir, Skrbic -- Petar Skrbic, and I," meaning General Mladic. "Officer promotions agreed upon." I can comment. It was just before the 28th of June, which was the patron saint's day of the Army of the VRS when officer promotions took place, and he discussed this with the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, could I show you the remainder of the entry before I ask for your comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I ask that we advance to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the portion of the -- this diary entry that the Prosecution is most interested in is the last line. Could I ask you to read that aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's at the top of the page of the -- could we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the rank of general, a promotion was decided upon for Sladoje, it was Colonel Cedo Sladoje. Then Dusan Kukobad [phoen], who was the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Then Miladin Prstojevic, Chief of Staff of the Herzegovina Corps for later. Others will be promoted, and then it doesn't say when. We have to -- we have to make or create something at Trnovo, although I can't make out what.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we now move to the last entry I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the last entry you want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One more entry, Your Honour, and then a one-minute video-clip, Your Honour, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we -- let me just check with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a bit of an unusual schedule. We'll -- if you'd finish, then we could skip the afternoon session. I'm looking at interpretation, transcription, and technicians, whether we could -- how much time would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's about ten questions, Your Honour. Please don't count. I'd have to count if you're going to hold me to ten, but I'm really on the last page of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we continue and so to save that we have to return this afternoon because I would need three minutes for reading a decision as well which is so urgent that we can't leave that until next week. Then under those circumstances. I'm also looking at you, Mr. Stanisic, it's a bit longer that we usually do. Is that -- would that -- I see that it apparently causes no such problem that we would have to refrain from doing it. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'd now ask you to look at 65 ter 5016.1, excerpt 7. It begins in the original with an ERN that ends in 536. And the entry that I want to draw your attention to is a -- records a meeting in Belgrade on the 30th of June, 1995. And are you able to see that entry?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you identify for us who the participants are?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I was in Drvar at the time, but let me just see if Mladic wrote down who was present. No, there are no notes about those present, perhaps at the bottom, but if he didn't note it down at the beginning he would hardly do it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the third page of this entry where we see at the top where -- I'm sorry, it's the second page. There's an entry for JS. When you've had an opportunity to see that, my question would be: After reading the entry, are you able to tell us who JS is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me -- JS, yes, I can see this is on the fifth line from the bottom. "JS: Which forces can be engaged by General Mrksic." I don't know, perhaps JS, these are somebody's initials. This is something that this JS said because then afterwards it -- it's written "JS" and a colon and what JS said is stated: "Which forces can General Mrksic engage." At the time General Mrksic was the commander of the Serbian army of the Krajina. So the question is being asked if the Army of the Serbian Krajina can be used for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to page 4 of this entry, and we see the initials JS again and there's a text immediately after JS. I'd ask you to read that aloud.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that fourth page. I can still see which forces can General Mrksic engage -- ah, I can see a little bit more now. Are you asking me to look at this JS again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you could read aloud just the first sentence of what is recorded as JS or after JS.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "My men should be taken into account in the utmost way when an operation is being planned. I have no confidence in Mile Novakovic, at least as far as competency or professionalism is concerned. The -- they have not given any assistance to the corps command for at least six months, and I have to ask that they be taken into account. My men were told the first day that they were paramilitaries. Pecanac should be informed" -- no, no, no, "Pecanac should be separated with 400 men, rest for seven days, and assign to General Mrksic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the last entry that I want you to read is -- or the last portion of this entry is on the last page, page 5, and there there are two passages after JS. Could I ask you to read both of what appears after the initials JS aloud?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There are two JS entries here. I'm reading the first one. "I can find 120 perfect men who would go there in seven days. These would be people from the eastern sector. That would be the support." And then again JS, and there was an M there that was crossed out with just the JS remaining. "They should not be engaged (we gave 80 from Erdut, we gave 80 from Djeletovci."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are you able to tell from the context what does the 80 refer to? Are we talking about 80 men? 80 cars? 80 weapons? Are you able to tell from the context what the 80, 80 from Erdut, 80 from Djeletovci?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this refers to men because the same JS says above that 120 perfect men were taken from the eastern sector and then they should not be engaged, because of this engaged. We gave 80 from Erdut, we gave 80 from Djeletovci. So he already has 160 men somewhere, so these 120 should not then be engaged for some task that was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, based on your experience and knowledge of the conflict, are you able to assist in what 80 men from Erdut might be referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably an operation or a preparation for an operation because I can see, when we were reading previous entries by JS, somebody was complaining that the corps commander of the Serbian army of the Krajina was not helping, and General Mile Novakovic was being charged with not working very well. So there was some kind of military operation that these men needed to be engaged in. Perhaps these were some 120 perfect men, were they perhaps specially trained soldiers or special formations. In any case, these seem to be some kind of special men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with respect to 80 from Djeletovci, would your answer be the same or do you -- based on your experience and knowledge of the conflict, are you able to be precise or more precise about what 80 men from Djeletovci might be referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We would need to find what was in Djeletovci, was it the police or the army that was stationed there. I don't know what was stationed there. This is not in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Erdut, I think, is somewhere in Baranja. I heard about that through the media, but I don't know anything about Djeletovci. I hadn't heard anything about that until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter Exhibit 5016.1. It is a set of seven excerpts from the larger diary of 5016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P394 is admitted into evidence. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, General, I'm going to ask you to look at approximately one minute of videotape. It is 65 ter 1167.1. The time code in this document is 1 hour, 39 minutes, and 29 seconds, to 1 hour, 40 minutes, and 16 seconds. I would ask you to pay particular attention to the vehicle we see and the uniforms that we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, having looked at the video, are you able to tell us whether the vehicle we see is a vehicle of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military TAM 110 vehicle. I didn't see the licence plates or the number, so I cannot really say whether it is a vehicle of the Army of Republika Srpska or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether the armed men we see in the video are wearing uniforms that identify them as soldiers in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They're not soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska because the Army of Republika Srpska did not -- or their soldiers did not wear red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the organisation that these men are associated with by looking at the uniforms they are wearing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I really couldn't say because different uniforms were worn. All I know is that the Army of Republika Srpska did not have any red berets. As for who wore red berets and whom I met in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina when I went there, that is something I really couldn't say who these people are because I don't have any other symbols other than the Serbian tricolour on the beret. But the Serbian tricolour was worn by the Army of Republika Srpska, by the Army of Yugoslavia, and, I don't know, perhaps the special police also wore that, from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if I may play you just a short clip from earlier on in the video where there is a clearer picture of the uniform, perhaps that will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Laugel to play from 2 minutes, 11 seconds, to 2 minutes, 51 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you stop at the point where you want to have a still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no sound in this video, General, so if you do want to make a comment as we view it or want us to freeze on any particular section, please just indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop. I can see the flag of a unit which was called the Skorpions, and I can recognise it by the emblem of the scorpion below the letters where it says "Skorpions." It's a little bit illegible, but this is the Skorpions unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there's no need to play the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you want me to play the remainder of the video before I tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've seen what I've seen. I'm usually not happy to ask to be -- to admit into evidence any portion which we have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I misspoke, I'm not seeking to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that it be marked for identification. The cameraman will be testifying later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you assign a number to it, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P395, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed. Well, Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock. And we're now certainly ten minutes beyond what we -- and I need some time as well. Could you finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, we see in the picture here that these men are wearing black uniforms and red berets. Based on your experience and knowledge of the conflict, was there any other unit that you observed wearing black uniforms and red berets?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no black uniforms and red berets in the territory of the Army of Republika Srpska. I'm not aware that any unit of the Army of Republika Srpska or of the police of Republika Srpska ever wore black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Any paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for paramilitary units, they disappeared in 1992 for the most part. The only ones that remained were two or three groups around Sarajevo. These were Vaske's Chetniks, Aleksic's Chetniks, and Manda's Chetniks. They didn't interfere or bother the army, but they were also not under the jurisdiction of the army, they were under the jurisdiction of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'd only be interested if there was a paramilitary group that you had seen wearing black uniforms and red berets. Did you ever see a paramilitary unit wearing a black uniform and a red beret in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Before I read a decision which has to be done in private session, Mr. Groome, I do understand that you would need another 15 minutes on Wednesday. Would that exclusively deal with the chart similar to the ones we have seen today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
